utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel and to everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager, Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. I'll now turn to Defence counsel for their appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stefane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for the other Defence team. I'm turning to Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura today, Rodney Dixon and Mr. Nermin Mulalic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber greets everyone present, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom. Today, Friday, the 14th, I must inform -- or I'd like to inform everyone that the legal officer, Stephanie Godart will be leaving us, and as she has been acting as a go-between between the parties and the Chamber I wanted to inform you of her departure. She'll be leaving today and she'll be replaced in the following days. Once we have decided on who our future legal officer will be. I wanted to inform you of this. In addition, I believe that there are new documents that we have to deal with, and Mr. Bourgon said that he wanted to take the floor to make submissions with regard to these documents. You may take the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. This is an oral motion to amend our list of exhibits, Mr. President. 24th of January was the last time it was amended, but when we met the witness, we expected today, a couple of days ago, he provided us with six documents that aren't included in our list or in the Prosecution's list. These are documents that we weren't able to obtain until now. So we have disclosed these six documents to the Prosecution. I don't believe they will be objecting to our motion. We are requesting that you grant us a lot of to use these documents this morning. These documents are documents from the municipality of Zenica and they relate to today's witness. We have provided a list to the Registrar. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to this motion, are there any objections that the Prosecution has to admitting these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We have no objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As the Judges don't see why this should present a problem, we take note of the motion and accept it. We will now call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I'd first like to make sure that you are receiving interpretation. If you can hear what I'm saying in your own language, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ramiz Dzaferovic. I was born on the 25th of March, 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the municipality of Visegrad, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you currently employed? And if so, what is the nature of your employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have my own company, which is -- which deals with auditing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you hold a position of any kind? If so, what kind of position, and for which institution did you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 1990 until the 17th of May, 1993, I was the director of a state company. From the 27th of May, 1993, until the 27th of May, 1994, I was the president of the executive authorities in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before in international or national court about the events in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I've appeared as a witness for a national or international court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down. Before I give the floor to Defence counsel, I would like to provide you with some brief information about the procedure we'll be following. You've been called as a witness for the Defence, and you will first have to answer the questions put to you by Defence counsel, whom you have certainly met already. Once this stage has been completed and we've been told that it should take about three-quarters of an hour, the Prosecution will put questions to you within the framework of what we call the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once this stage has been concluded, Defence counsel may ask you additional questions that relate to questions put to you in the course of the cross-examination. The three Judges sitting before you, according to the Rules of Procedure, may put questions to you at any time, but to ensure that the proceedings run smoothly, the Judges prefer to wait for the parties to conclude their examination before intervening. You will notice that the questions are of a different kind. When Defence counsel puts questions to you in the course of their examination-in-chief, they must make sure that they don't put leading questions to you. When the Prosecution cross-examines you, they are allowed to put leading questions to you. The Judges sitting before you will put questions to you, the objective of which is to help to establish the truth. The Judges put questions to you to assess the value of your testimony, and not on behalf of either of the parties. In order to do this, they may put questions to you that may not be leading. So roughly speaking, this is the procedure we'll be following. When questions are put to you, the parties might show you documents and ask you to comment on them and ask you whether you can recognise them. This is something that might happen. If you fail to understand a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Sometimes the questions can be very long, and one might lose one's bearings. If that's the case, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase the question. We have no written documents concerning your testimony, so your oral answers are extremely important, because that constitutes your testimony. Try to answer the questions as fully as possible and as precisely as possible. I would also like to point out that as you have taken the solemn declaration and said that you will speak the truth, you should not give false testimony. I hope you're fully aware of this fact. And in addition, I would also like to point out that a witness may refuse to answer a question if the witness believes that his answer may cause him problems at a subsequent date, because the answer might provide information that could be used to incriminate the witness. In such exceptional circumstances, we have had no such cases to date, but nevertheless I must point it out, in such exceptional circumstances, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question. If this is done, you are granted a form of immunity. This is how we will be proceeding. If you encounter any difficulties, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact. We are here to deal with any difficulties you may run into. I will now give the floor to the Defence, who will commence with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dzaferovic. In addition to what the Presiding Judge has just informed you of, I would also like to ask you to make a brief pause when I put a question to you, before answering the question. This will enable the interpreters to interpret what is said and it will enable everyone in the courtroom to follow our exchange. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, what are you by profession, and could you tell us something about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I graduated -- I have graduated in economy and I'm an auditor. I have about 22 years of professional experience, mostly obtained in financial institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since I'd like to start using documents immediately when examining the witness, I would now like to ask the usher to distribute these documents to the witness, the Trial Chamber, and to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told the Presiding Judge that you were appointed the president of the executive council of the town of Zenica towards the end of May 1993. Can you please look at document number 1 in the bundle and tell me first what this document represents. And secondly, can you confirm that this indeed is the date when you were appointed to the duty that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I was appointed by the Presidency of the municipality of Zenica. I was appointed on the 17th of May, and I was given 13 days to select the local government. And it is true that my appointment was finally confirmed on the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was this published? What kind of document is this? Where were decisions of the War Presidency and other civilian bodies published?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: This is the Official Gazette of the municipality of Zenica, so such decisions were published at all public places, and even on the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, could you please look at the first document published in the Official Gazette, and the decision is Decision on the Establishment of the Presidency of the Municipal Assembly of Zenica. Can you please tell me: Who were members of the War Presidency of Zenica? Does this decision reflect what this body was composed of?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is very precise. When this decision was established, before that, there was the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Zenica that was in place, and after that, the Presidency of the municipality of Zenica was established, and it was made up of the president of the municipality, the president of the executive council of the municipality of Zenica, the chief of defence of Zenica, the chief of police station, the commander of the Territorial Defence staff, and presidents of the groups of the parliamentary parties in the municipality of Zenica. After that, the municipality parliament adopted that and the Presidency was authorised by the Municipal Assembly to pass decisions between sessions, and those decisions would then be ratified at the sessions of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Here, it says that a member of the War Presidency is the commander of the staff of the civilian defence. Tell me: Was the civilian defence a civilian body?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a civilian body. It had a dual responsibility. By hierarchy, it was responsible to the municipal staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, and according to the vertical hierarchy, it was responsible to the municipal parliament, or in other words, to the municipal government of the municipality of Zenica. The same went for the chief of police in Zenica, and the same went for the chief of national defence in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, did the commanders of the military structures of the municipal defence staff or military units, pursuant to this decision, were they members of the War Presidency, as a civilian body of authority in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, Mr. Dzaferovic: Did military bodies, or in other words, units, at any point in time when you were the president of the municipal government or a citizen of Zenica, as such, were they ever superior? Did they ever establish military control over Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm now going to ask you to tell me, Mr. Dzaferovic: What was the situation in Zenica in 1993? What problems did the town of Zenica face at that time, given the war conditions during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: When I was appointed the president of the executive body of government of the municipality of Zenica, and at the moment when I took over my duties, Zenica had already been blocked for four months. During that period, Zenica had about 120.000 inhabitants, and it gave shelter to about 47.000 refugees and expelled persons from all areas or municipalities of the then Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In a nutshell, one may say that there were two towns in one town. The 47.000 refugees had needs. They had to be accommodated. They had to be fed and clothed and so on and so forth. They were accommodated in 49 camps in the entire territory of the municipality of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, can you please look at document number 4, and can you please tell me whether you recognise this document. If you do recognise it, can you please tell us why you brought it here.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it. At a session of the municipal government which took place on the 4th June, 1993 -- before I say anything else, if you will allow me, I would like to say that the make-up of the municipal government was a multi-ethnic. Out of the 11 members of the municipal government, six were Bosniaks, three were Croats, one was Serb, and one was Slovenian. As I continue answering your questions, I would like to say that all the decisions that were taken during my 14 months of duty, the municipal government was in session every day, and all the decisions in 99 per cent were brought by consensus and ratified first by the Executive Council and then by the Municipal Assembly of Zenica. Since the town at that period was facing a large number of refugees and expelled persons, the Executive Council started drafting a programme aimed at survival. We outlined our needs for food, washing agents, and all the facilities that were necessary for the work of companies in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, I asked you to look at conclusion number 4. You Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond have just told us that there were a lot of refugees in Zenica. Can you please tell us whether the refugees kept on coming. Were you at all in a position to know how many people there were in Zenica at any given point in time?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: During the war, refugees kept on coming from all the areas and municipalities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Many international organisations attempted to establish the actual situation. However, it was very difficult. Our estimates helped us to establish the factual condition on the ground, when we had to introduce rationing in food. People kept on coming day in and day out. There were 5.600 refugees that arrived on one single day, around 1.00 in the night, and they were accommodated in the schools in Zenica. However, at that point in time, the international community was already involved and continued working until the end of February 1994. By that time, they opened about 14 camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 3. You started talking about the blockade of Zenica which had lasted for four months when the government embarked on drafting a survival programme. Can you tell me: Do you recognise this document? What is this document about, and what were the problems that Zenica faced at the time when hampered its survival?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that the survival programme envisioned all the needs for food, energy sources, and materials for the work of public companies. We wanted to get in touch with international humanitarian organisations, primarily with UNHCR. We tried to seek solutions that would help us to survive this difficult situation. The blockade was getting ever tighter. We tried to centralise all the food that existed at the time in Zenica. These actions were channelled through two channels. First of all, we wanted to provide food for all the local population and the refugees. Most of the food came from the UNHCR. We wanted to centralise all available food and focus it in one place, in the direction for commodity reserves. That was the first activity. We received approval from all the international institutions, including local humanitarian organisations, such as the Red Cross, Caritas, Merhamet, and others. The second activity was aimed at looking at the arable fields that could be used for sowing, and then we wanted to provide mechanisation that could help with that, and we also wanted to look at mills. At that time, everything was haphazard. Nothing went continuously. The energy sources were scarce. Citizens were given coupons for rationed supply, and one of the things we did, we provided them with wood and coal as an alternative energy resource.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, before this Trial Chamber, there is a report by Mr. Thebault dating to May 1993. In his report, he says that during that period of time, only 5 per cent of the required necessities reached Zenica. As the president of the Zenica government, can you tell us what quantities of food were at that time supplied to the citizens? What problems did you face with that regard?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, when we decided to draft this survival programme for the city of Zenica, we thought that this was a security issue more than anything else. We introduced rationed supplies, and all the citizens of Zenica received identical quantities of everything. Together with the UNHCR, we established what one-fifth of the needs would be, one-fifth of the bare necessities for the survival of every citizen. That was 500 grammes of flour per capita. We were aware of the situation that faced both us and the international organisations, which could not enter the town with their convoys. We're talking about the month of September, the 6th or 7th month into the complete blockade of the town. In order to keep peace and order in town, we embarked on this step. However, these were only our estimates. In November 1993, every citizen received approximately 80 grammes of flour. Even that one-fifth that was envisaged for the citizens was reduced, one-tenth. One may say that the food that was used by the citizens of Zenica can be compared with what a mouse would need for its survival. I would like to emphasise before this Trial Chamber that in the month of December, the staple food of our citizens was potato and flour came in very sparse quantities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 5, Mr. Dzaferovic. Given the situation that Zenica and all its inhabitants were in, would you say that this is one of the documents by which you tried to draw the attention of the international community to such a difficult situation?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: This is just one in the series of documents. We wanted Mr. Philippe Morillon to visit Zenica. We asked for their attention. We held a press conference, attended by all the representatives of the international community who were there at the time. Mr. Martin Garrod, who was a European monitor in the territory of Zenica at that time, was also there. We asked from the representatives of international organisations to talk to the governments of their respective countries. We wanted Zenica to be officially proclaimed a town under blockade, and we wanted food to be air-dropped to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before this Trial Chamber, there is document P181, in which General Garrod describes a meeting that he held with you personally. In this document, he says that at that meeting, it was said that the humanitarian situation was bordering on a total disaster. Zenica had 200.000 inhabitants, out of whom 47.000 were refugees. You received 40 tonnes of aid a month, which sufficed only for five days' survival of the entire population. Would this part of the report, which describes your conversation with Mr. Garrod, represent a correct description of the situation in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was at the moment when we held that conversation. However, things got worse after that. The first humanitarian convoy entered Zenica sometime in February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, can you please look at document number 7. It's pages 26 and 27. You said that you had organised a conference, an international conference, involving representatives of the international community. I apologise. The pages in question are -- first look at page number 1. Can you tell me if you know who the author of this book is? It says Besim Spahic here?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: He's the president of the Presidency of the municipality of Zenica. He was the presiding [indiscernible] of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I asked you to look at pages 26 and 27, and before I put the question to you, can you please tell me whether certain international officials arrived and visited Zenica upon your invitation? If you can remember: Who was it who came and faced the dire situation that you had to face in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: It is very difficult to remember. However, Mr. Jakovic arrived. He was the American ambassador. And sometime in December as far as I can remember there was the present high commissioner, Lord Paddy Ashdown. He visited the refugee camps in Bandol, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this international press conference that you have just mentioned, can you tell me whether it was attended by journalists from the best-known press agencies? Did you tackle the situation that was facing Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that press conference, we declared that the situation was alarming and that the survival of people was in question. They were threatened. The functioning of business and trade in the city was also threatened. I requested that international organisations were -- in fact not even international organisations could leave Zenica because it was under blockade, and they requested that I, as the president of the executive committee head the convoy, in order to save the town, but they couldn't guarantee security or help their representatives in international humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On page 19, 20, and 21, have a look at page 19, 20, and 21, and were these in fact -- was this in fact the nature of the exchanges you had Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond with the international community and the warnings that you gave them?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, as far as this subject is concerned, tell me whether at that time the citizens also came under fire. Was Zenica shelled? Was fire opened? Did people die as a result?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we advanced very slightly, but I think much progress was made in terms of security in Zenica. The Executive Committee launched an initiative and the Presidency of the municipality of Zenica adopted this, and the parliament also confirmed it. A committee for human rights was to be formed in June 1993. We suggested that in the committee for human rights, there should be members who were reliable and who would be trusted by all the three constituent peoples. Representatives of the Croatian, Serbian, and Muslim communities should be there. As far as I can remember, that committee was composed of Mr. Jakov Montiljo. He was the president of the committee. And there were members of the clergy. There was Father Radic, who represented the Catholic Church. Then there was the head imam of the Islamic community, Mr. Dautovic, and there was the representative of the Orthodox Church, whose name I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document number 6, please. Do you recognise this document, and is this the document that you have just been referring to?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And let me just add something else. Mr. Drincic, the representative of the Orthodox Church, was also a member. This is one of the documents the purpose of which was to improve the situation in the state and to gain trust, because there was fierce fighting around the municipality of Zenica. As far as I can remember, a conscientious objection was an idea that was accepted. Citizens who didn't want to bear arms could participate in activities to assist the defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, what was the attitude towards all religions in the town? And could you please comment on document number 2.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: The municipal government, in cooperation with the Presidency of Zenica municipality and with the parliament too, took decisions that were important for all the citizens. The purpose of these decisions was to improve the security situation in the town. The Executive Committee also adopted a decision and declared that there should be religious holidays for all three religions. And during these festivities, these people would not have to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, a minute ago you were speaking about the composition of the Executive Committee, which was at all times multi-ethnic. Tell me: Who was the president of the committee for human rights?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Jakov Montiljo, who is still alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was his nationality?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was a Jew.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the composition of the municipal organs of administration of the entire municipality, and did it in any way threaten the multi-ethnic composition of Zenica, in spite of the fact that you were living in very difficult wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the composition of the Executive Committee in 1993 was identical to its composition in 1975. As far as I can remember, the number of people employed in the municipality of Zenica was about 240. I think there were about 30 per cent of Croatian representatives, and 70 per cent were Serbs and Bosniaks. There were also Slovenians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the protection of religious rights, religious freedom, please have a look at document 7, page 36, item 2. In the middle, it starts with the words -- at the end of that paragraph it says: "In the course of the war, not a single religious building or place of worship was destroyed." Have a look at the text and can you tell me whether this reflects the truth, whether this reflects the situation in Zenica, and what was your attitude towards religious buildings and members of the clergy?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. At the initiative of the local authorities --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I was referring to the Bosnian version, page 36, second paragraph. It starts with the words "Mr. Kenney pointed out." So whoever has the English or French version will be able to follow what I have been asking the witness about. It's page 10 in the translation. So could you please tell me, given what it says here -- what is stated here, is this correct, and what was your attitude towards religious buildings and members of the clergy?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. At the initiative of the Executive Committee and in cooperation with representatives of the Catholic Church, with Mr. Radic in particular, we launched an initiative to renovate the monument to Our Lady, which was destroyed in the '50s, and in addition to that request, there was a request from Father Radic. He wanted the building that was adjacent to the Church of St. Ilija -- in fact, there were four or five flats in that building, and he asked the Executive Committee to make those flats available for the security of the institution. The citizens lived in those premises before the war too. We did this too. So about the 15th of August, when the statue of Our Lady was revealed, Father Petar Andjelovic attended that ceremony, and as far as these monstrous lies are concerned, which were very harmful -- well, he said that he could testify to the fact that 12 Croats hadn't been hanged there. His presence testified to that fact. The conditions weren't ideal, because there was a war. But this was a fact that couldn't be ignored.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzaferovic. Tell me whether everything you have just said, since it was a war, tell me whether Zenica was shelled from enemy positions.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For that reason, the local authorities created markets and created conditions to sell goods in enclosed areas. As far as I remember, the town market, which had a capacity for about 700 to a thousand men, if that market hadn't been relocated, I can claim with full responsibility that there would have been a massacre. But thankfully, that didn't happen, given what the municipal authorities did at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, the market in the town was shelled from enemy positions.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Another brief question: Since you said that there was the security issue, et cetera, did you encounter problems of theft, and together with the civilian and military organs, did you establish a form of cooperation to deal with that problem, to the extent it was possible, given the conditions in Zenica? Were there any policies pursued by the civilian and military authorities to crack down on all forms of crime in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A committee was formed in Zenica for the security of the town. It was composed of all the representatives, all local and regional representatives. It was composed of organs responsible to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the president of the municipal court, of the high court, the representative of the MUP, of the Ministry of the Interior, representative of the ABiH, or rather, the 3rd Corps; a representative of the committee for human rights. There were many problems. The town was under a blockade, and there was the problem of food. There was the fight for survival.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, could you please tell me whether the Executive Committee also had the problem of controlling foreigners. Was it impossible for them to control foreigners? And did you issue orders or assign tasks stating that this issue had to be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Executive Committee in Zenica adopted a conclusion and proposed to the Presidency in Zenica and to the parliament that this conclusion be adopted and that certain measures be taken. As far as I can remember, on the 17th of October, 1993, the Executive Committee proposed a conclusion. And since the situation in Zenica was alarming, given the presence of certain individuals in Zenica or given the fact that certain individuals were passing through Zenica, individuals in uniform who were Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond abusing insignia, who were falsely [Realtime transcript read in error "forcefully"] identifying themselves, the judicial authorities weren't functioning properly, the organs of prosecution weren't functioning properly, et cetera. So we came to the conclusion that human rights were threatened to such an extent that they might just be wiped out, and the functioning of Zenica was at risk. In order to improve the situation, since we respected the idea that responsibilities should be shared, we requested that the MUP establish or obtain information on foreigners in Zenica, on foreigners entering and leaving Zenica. We requested that the ABiH, or rather, the 3rd Corps, ensure that members of the military didn't pass through the town with their rifles. We asked the judicial authorities and organs of prosecution to do everything they could to improve the situation in the town. And I was talking about this period a minute ago. In October, citizens were receiving the minimum of food necessary to survive. And again, not even a mouse could have survived on such rations. And these efforts resulted in improvement in the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Whose responsibility were the foreigners, and who did you ask to record their movement?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: We asked the Ministry of the Interior to do this, and they're responsible to the Ministry of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Just for the sake of the transcript, there is the word "forcefully" on page 20, line 23. But the witness said "falsely." So could that be improved. The word was not "forcefully" but "falsely." My last question, Mr. Dzaferovic, concerns the fact that in Zenica there was a building that is referred to in the indictment in this case. As president of the Executive Committee, did you ever hear about the issue of the music school or did you obtain any information in an indirect way?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was interviewed by a radio station, this issue was raised. I established contact with the 3rd Corps about this, and they said that this concerned the military police of the 7th Muslim. And in the 14 months that I occupied the post of the president of the Executive Committee, I intervened on two or three occasions. I was seen by the president, and as president, in fact, I saw about 5.600 citizens. There was someone called Mr. Jonjic, or rather, his mother who came to see me. She complained that her son had disappeared. I told the chief of cabinet to check this through the security of the 7th Muslim. I was told that he was in the penal and correctional facility, in the KP Dom, which was where people had been convicted were serving their sentence. And then there was the case of Mr. Viskovic, whose wife also came to see me to ask me to find where he was, find out where he was. And then acting directly, I checked the information and found out that he had previously been the chief of the security service. That was before the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I found out that he would be released after he had been interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How far is the music school from your office? Did you have to pass that way? Did you ever personally see anybody being brought in or ill-treated in the school?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I already tried to explain this to the representatives of the international community. For example, Mr. Martin Garrod asked me the same question. Music school is a very small facility, some hundred metres away from the municipality, where my office was, where the offices of the Executive Council were. He also said that people were being taken there and ill-treated. To answer your question: The music school is in the very close vicinity of the higher court, of the municipal court, of the Croatian hall, of the bank, the municipality building, the national theatre. It is in the very centre of the town of Zenica. And by the logic of things, if things like that had been happening, Zenica, which has 83 local communes, this could not have happened. I am not talking about why people were being taken anywhere. I did not seek to establish that, because it was not my duty. The responsibility of the local government was to provide the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina with materiel and technical assistance and help them with mobilising people. I believe that this is just nothing but terrible propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the KP Dom? Did you ever establish the conditions that your co-citizens were kept in there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Ten days into my mandate, I went there with my colleagues. We visited the KP Dom. And finally, at the end of the day, this institution was supplied from the direction for commodity reserves. I spoke directly with Mr. Jonjic. I even remember this conversation. I knew this person personally. And he told me that he had had problems in the armed formation that he belonged to, that he was expelled. And he said that he was not good for any of the sides. He was exchanged some ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzaferovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm turning towards the Prosecution for their cross-examination, unless Mr. Dixon has questions. Mr. Dixon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There is one matter that we do wish to clarify. It might simply be a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sir, if you could recall at line 4 of page 22, you mentioned that you will saw about 5.600 citizens in your capacity. Could you confirm that in fact when you mentioned that figure, you were talking about seeing those persons for various reasons, not only in relation to prison or detention facilities? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. During those 14 months, I saw about 5.600 people, and I believe that this can be checked in the documents of the municipality. They came to me with different issues. In 99 per cent, they asked me, without food, when the convoys were arriving, whether they would be able to survive. They talked to me about their fear of helplessness and despair.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, sir. Your Honour, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzaferovic. First of all, I followed carefully what you initiated as president of the Executive Council, and it was very interesting to see that in tab 2, the conclusions you initiated, or you made, 31st of May, 1993, the first number, when you regulated these holidays and that you took account of all religious groups, it's almost like the UN holidays we have here, so the different Catholic and Muslim holidays. So that was very interesting to see that again. But let me go back to what you said just now about the music school. First, I think you acknowledged that you were told by international observers, I believe you mentioned Mr. Garrod, that there were mistreatments in the music school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I had ongoing contacts with all the representatives. I can, for example, mention Mr. La Mota, Mr. Larry, and other European monitors. They also heard that allegedly people were being ill-treated in this music school. I tried to explain a while ago where the music school was. On any given day, at least a thousand people passed by that school. I myself passed by it. I was looking at it from my office. Believe me, there are documents in the municipality of Zenica, and people who worked with me, all the secretaries who participated in the work. And it is not only owing to our work, but -- and not only to my work, but to our national team. I told Mr. Garrod: Why don't we take a straw unannounced to see who we will find there? He refused to do that. In 14 months, I had only two interventions. The first one was by a woman, whom I personally knew, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond about my neighbour, whom I personally knew, and also there was another intervention by a woman whom I didn't know personally, but I did check to see what was going on with her son, because I also have a mother, and I knew what this was -- how she must have felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We heard evidence in this case, and I quote it: "The whole city was rife with rumours about the music school, the music school being a detention camp." That's Judge Adamovic. And there was other information from ICRC, ECMM, UNHCR, about what happened there. And you are saying that's all terrible propaganda?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I say. You're mentioning Mr. Adamovic. He was a military judge. We had constant contacts, and he never said anything to me about that. We were even friends after that. I claim with full responsibility that this was not a camp. People may have been interrogated there, but this was not a camp. This is a facility in the very centre of Zenica, across the road from the music school there is a supreme court, where there were Croats, Bosnians, and Serbs working. Across the road from there was the Croatian hall, which was secured by the Croatian police. There is also a commercial bank and the new school -- the new building of the municipality, the old building of the municipality, there is a theatre. So on a daily basis, through the park where that building was, a thousand people walked. And if that had been happening on a large scale, this would be known. I worked with my colleagues until very late in the night, sometimes until 2.00 or 3.00. We had 298 sessions during the four [as interpreted] months that I was in my position. Sometimes we had two sessions a day. So if all this had been happening, we would have known that. As I sit here today before this Trial Chamber, I don't know whether I could have worked better than I did. We worked -- we did whatever we could. The objection of consciousness is now being introduced in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they have been talking about that for two years. But there is nothing I can say about that with regard my work and the work of my colleagues during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not disputing that. But if it was so public, so publicly accessible, the music school, why was the ICRC prevented from visiting that school? Can you give us an explanation? That would have been the best way to refute all this propaganda, to allow the ICRC to see that facility. Why wasn't that happening, Mr. Dzaferovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I have never heard this before. I am prepared to face the person who told you that, who told you that the ICRC was prevented from entering that facility. Forty international organisations, Mr. Larry, Mr. -- let me not mention any more names. They all spoke to me. I personally offered to go there with them. It would have taken us five minutes to go there. I personally offered them to go and visit that facility. The military police was there, so I do not exclude the possibility that people were being interrogated there. However, during the 14 months that I was there, when I was appointed the president of the Executive Council, I had hope. I showed courage when I introduced rationing of food. And people were absolutely certain that they would all receive the same quantity of food. The questionnaire that was used to establish how many people there were in Zenica, you will not find any questions about the ethnic affiliation of the citizens of Zenica, and you can find that document in the archives of the municipality of Zenica. I assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I apologise to interrupt, but in light of the answer that the witness has given to my learned friend's question, I don't know if he's going to take this any further, but he has made an allegation that the Red Cross was not permitted to enter the music school. And I do wish to know on what basis he makes such an allegation. Because from our reading of the evidence to date, there's no such evidence before Your Honours that the Red Cross could not enter the music school. And the witness has now confirmed that he has no knowledge of that fact either. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That was my next point, and Mr. Dixon has document P371 in front of him. And Your Honours, it's annex C. And I would like the witness to have a look at that, and perhaps it could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Witness, unfortunately, we don't have a B/C/S version of it, but it's very short, and I can read it out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's an annex to a report by Charles McLeod, and this one page, and I'll read the title and the date. It dates 7th May, 1993. Title: "Meeting with Jean-Luc Noverraz head of the ICRC, Zenica." "Comment: Since access to prisons was a major concern and ECMM was making progress as a result of its strong contacts, I wanted to make sure that we were doing -- that what we were doing was coordinated with ICRC. The key points from a short and friendly meeting are as follows:," next paragraph, "I asked what access ICRC have to prisoners in Zenica. He said that they only have access to the main prison, not to the MUP or music school." That's document number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me continue with a second document, and this is document P670, by Mr. Delic. And I'll just quote from it, P670. And unfortunately, I haven't prepared that, but because this seems to be an issue, I would like to support the ICRC documentation or the reference with another one coming from the ABiH. It dates Sarajevo, 14th August, 1993, so about three months after this first document. And it's signed by the commander of the ABiH, Rasim Delic. The heading is "to BH army, 3rd Corps command." First paragraph: "The International Committee of the Red Cross mission in Sarajevo has drawn our attention to the problems that their delegates are facing in the Zenica area." Next paragraph: "According to the ICRC, as part of their routine prison visits, the Zenica ICRC has attempted on several occasions to visit the prisoners, who fall under the jurisdiction of the 7th Brigade of the BH army, 3rd Corps, and are detained in the prison in the former secondary music school in Zenica. Except for one visit in May 1993, the ICRC has constantly been denied access to the prisoners detained with the 7th Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Doesn't that establish from two different sources, one even the army of the ABiH, that they had, except for one occasion sometime between May and August 1993, no access to the music school?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I have no information of that kind. They didn't contact me personally. But what you have just read out about the camp, I don't know if there's more than 40 square metres of available space on those premises. So what kind of a camp could that have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you ever entered the music school?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I have. We visited the music school, I and Mr. Brane Ivanovic and Huso Smailovic. We saw two policemen there, two military policemen, and the commander, who was ill and he was in the second part of that building. A clinic was also located in that part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was the commander's name?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: His name was Halid Brazina. He was a deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And deputy commander of what?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: He was assistant commander for logistics in the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned an acquaintance of yours, Mr. Viskovic. Is that Mr. Anto Viskovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Anto Viskovic, yes, the former chief of the CSB at the security services centre before the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you know what MOS means, M-O-S?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. Given the propaganda that was spread throughout the war, obviously all Bosniaks were considered to be members of the Muslim forces, of the Mujahedin, of the MOS, et cetera, et cetera. So this is a term that many abused, in terms of providing military information on the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did the MOS ever guard your building, your apartment Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond building, in that relevant time, while you were president of the Executive Council of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why they would have guarded my building. I think that information is false. I had a security that had been officially assigned to me, a municipal security, the civilian police provided security for me and for others in the municipality. Throughout the wartime period, I moved around freely, as an ordinary citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just read out what Mr. Viskovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Before my learned friend does that, if I could intervene. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe he's going to read from a statement of Mr. Viskovic, which was never disclosed to the Defence, and I believe that this is a statement which the Defence have only received for the first time very recently, in fact, today. This is a witness who has not testified before the Tribunal, and this statement, in our submission, should not be allowed to be put to the witness. It's not a statement that the witness has made, to seek to cross-examine him on his credibility or to refresh his memory, but it's a statement of another witness who is not before the Tribunal. So in our submission, the Prosecution should only be allowed to put to the witness questions about his meetings and interactions with Mr. Viskovic or relatives of him, and not ask him questions about statements that were made by the witness, in a statement which was taken as long ago as 2001. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I could briefly respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As far as I know the Rules about cross-examination in this place, and perhaps elsewhere, is that I can certainly test the credibility of a witness with any credible, we believe, credible information we have. I'm allowed to put that to him, and he can say it's true or it's not true. And we have no obligation to disclose these statements. It's not Rule 68. And it wasn't a Prosecution witness who would testify. So under the disclosure Rules, we need not disclose it. I did it as a courtesy last night, to one Defence team, and to Mr. Dixon this morning. But I'm certainly allowed to put these allegations to this witness and see what he has to say in terms of credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As far as this issue is concerned, the Trial Chamber has already rendered its decision, with regard to whether the Prosecution can use documents that haven't been tendered into evidence. It suffices to consult the transcript, but I think it's already been said that if the Prosecution wants to present a new document, they should disclose this document to the Defence at least 24 hours in advance, so that the Defence can state his position in good time. We also said that if it's a matter of verifying the credibility of a witness, the parties could use documents of all kinds. That was the gist of our decision. It's half past 10.00. We, the Judges, will discuss the issue again. We've already decided on it, but it's always useful to discuss such problems. And we will resume at about 5 to 11.00, unless there is something the Prosecution would like to say before we leave. I'll give you the floor now again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to clarify: We don't want to use this document as an exhibited. I just would like to read out a small portion of a witness statement of a person Mr. Dzaferovic knows. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry. If I could just clarify one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: This is a statement which is actually not in evidence. That was the point that I was trying to make. And I have no objection to my learned friend cross-examining the witness about what happened in a particular meeting or where he lived. But I fail to see the purpose of putting a portion of a statement which is not in evidence, either through 92 bis or through the witness coming to testify. Your Honours would not have seen this statement. It's not going to be part of the record. And there is, in our submission, no purpose in doing it. My learned friend is free to cross-examine him about what happened and to put various assertions to him, but indeed not, and he should not show the statement to him. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now adjourn and we will resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. As I said, we have deliberated about the issue again. Naturally, we confirm our previous oral decision, and we will allow the Prosecution to refer to the document, the contents of which we are not familiar with, but the document won't be tendered into evidence. As far as testing the witness's credibility is concerned, the Prosecution may use a document that they have. You may read the part of the document that you wanted to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, I just wanted to read out one paragraph. It's five lines of what Mr. Anto Viskovic told an investigator about the conversation related to you. "During this period, I was effectively under house arrest. The building I was living in was watched by members of the MOS 24 hours a day. I complained about this to Ramiz Dzaferovic, president of the Executive Board of Zenica municipality. Dzaferovic also had an apartment in the same building, and he told me not to worry, saying 'the MOS are there to protect me as much as they are there to guard you.'" Do you have to make a comment about that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I can comment on that. It's true that it's door-to-door. There is a building, and I think Mr. Viskovic lived on the third floor. We were friends and we see each other today as well. Even when he left Bosnia and Herzegovina after the war, he sent a parcel to my children. As far as securing the entrance to the building in which I lived is concerned, well, that is not correct. That information is not correct. I had security that was provided for me in the municipality where I worked. I didn't have my own personal security officers. I didn't know who was on duty providing security in the municipal building in Zenica. But it was the police, or some policemen, who were engaged in providing the security, and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you didn't say these words, as quoted by Mr. Viskovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me finish --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: We spoke about other subjects, but that's not something he told me. Because -- I apologise, but the building I lived in was a building in which there were Serbs and Croats, and across the road from that building there were other functionaries. I, as the president of the Executive Committee, can confirm, and all other citizens can confirm, that I moved around in a normal manner, although I had certain unpleasant situations. I was even physically assaulted, not by Croats but by members of the Bosniak community. Children were maltreated, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me finish with the jobs you had, apart from your position in the Executive Council. I believe you responded to a question by His Honour Judge Antonetti that you were the director of a public company before you became president. What company was that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: It's the textile company, Kimo, Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was it producing textiles, clothes?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Clothes, sports clothes. And later, military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: During the wartime, it was producing military uniforms? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That was quite a profitable enterprise, I take it.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: No. That company was mobilised by the region to defend the country, and throughout the war it worked for defence purposes, right up until the conflict with the HVO, and it continued working after the conflict. Because the company was a multi-ethnic one, and when I left the company, Akrapovic, Jakob became the director and he still is, that post in Zenica. That was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So when you were director, was it a good personal enterprise for you? Did you profit from being the director of that company, financially?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: How would I profit, since there was a war? The purpose was to assist in defending the country. And when it was mobilised by governmental organs, material that wasn't appropriate was used to make uniforms. Uniforms were made out of blankets, tent material, ordinary textile, et cetera. Up until July 1992, there were about 400 workers. But later, because of the war, there were about two brigades working there. That would be between 120 and 150 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ever hold office after your Presidency over the Executive Council in Sarajevo, as chief of the federation tax department?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: No. After I left the post of president of the Executive Committee, I moved to the Kimo company again and remained there until June 1996. I was then elected as president of the republican administration for revenue in Bosnia and Herzegovina. After the Dayton Agreement had been signed, I was elected as the general director of the general revenue administration, and we organised the work of the federal revenue administration. And according to the Dayton Agreement, this included the revenue from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I remained in that post until the year 2000. I was then replaced by the High Representative, Mr. Wolfgang Petritsch. There was no factual basis for this replacement. My human rights were then violated and this is something I can claim before this Chamber. The international convention on human rights wasn't respected, and two years later, I think that was sometime in August, I was released. But there is such legally valid decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you, in fact, when you say you were replaced, you were basically fired by Mr. Wolfgang Petritsch, on grounds, and I quote, that you "failed to ensure the highest standards of non-political professionalism, thereby undermining the objectives of the Brussels peace implementation council and public confidence in your agency and in the economic reform process." And in the official letter you received, there was even allegations of corruption. Do you remember having received a letter from Mr. Wolfgang Petritsch stating those reasons for your removal?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received that decision on the 27th of February, 2000. These explanations were provided and according to the explanations, certain things were alleged. But the allegations weren't the real reason for replacing me. The High Representative, and the public in Bosnia and Herzegovina, fully aware of the real reasons for replacing me, but this is not something I would like to talk about. With the leave of the Chamber, I'd like to say: How can a man be replaced if there is no normal procedure followed and if an official isn't interviewed about this? I was a federal functionary, but I received such a document, in which I was to be replaced, and it was stated that, allegedly, an accusation had been confirmed, an accusation from the federal court. And this was quite false. I had never been convicted, and an indictment had never been brought against me at the federal court. But Wolfgang Petritsch is fully aware of the real reason for which I was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you say that Mr. Wolfgang Petritsch was fully aware of the real reasons, were you ever, by him or his successor, I believe was Mr. Ashdown, whom I believe you said you met as well, reinstated into your position?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't even make such a request. But if you insist, I can tell you why.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were you also banned, in the same letter you received, did it say that you were banned from holding public office, and did that remain in place until today?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it is in place now too. There was no trial, no procedure of any kind was followed. My rights were violated, and unfortunately, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I am now a second-class citizen. You, as an expert, will be able to see, on the basis of that decision, that no procedure of any kind was followed, and certain things weren't respected. There were certain allegations made. I was appointed as the general of the federation tax department, where I found 40 people, and I unified both entities and formed an institution that had 1.400 workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that the Dayton Agreement empowered the High Representative to take certain steps, steps like this, removal of senior officers in Bosnia? That was within his mandate?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such authorisation. His role was to assist, not to remove people, not to cut people's heads off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it would be best to stop there, because his testimony doesn't have to do with the public finance or the Dayton Agreement, but it has to do with what the municipality did in respect of the refugees. So it would be best to focus on the purpose of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It was my last question. We believe it affects his credibility. The allegations, as it states, I don't know more. The witness, I'm sure, knows more. But as it states on that decision the witness referred to, corruption was mentioned. I believe that's important for Your Honours to know. And I have that decision here. It's taken from the Internet. It's public. I don't know whether it's necessary. It's available for Your Honours if you want it. But I would not seek to tender it at this moment. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll now give the floor to Defence counsel, if they have additional questions to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Although you quite rightly pointed out that the questions put to the witness were not appropriate, given the role of the witness today, since the Prosecution has mentioned the Kimo company the witness worked in, and since they mentioned the charges on the basis of which the High Representative decided to replace this witness, the witness was replaced for corruption. I just have two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, because of not having paid tax, were proceedings instituted against you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I was released, and it would be good to have the judgement here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you haven't been convicted of anything, and this is -- although it states the contrary in the decision of the High Representative?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've never been convicted. I wouldn't be able to perform my duties as an auditor. The document states that no one can work as an auditor if a person has been convicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's go back to some questions that my learned colleague put to you earlier on. You were asked about a Red Cross visit to the music school. You said that the International Committee of the Red Cross never contacted you. Tell me: If they had contacted you, would you have done everything you could have done to provide them with access to the music school or any other buildings?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. I received over 200 representatives of international organisations while I was in office. I suggested that we go to certain buildings they wanted to visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of documents that you were shown by my colleague, you can see that it states that they in fact visited the music school on one Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond occasion, in May. If someone had already visited the building, was there any reason, while you were the president of the Executive Committee, to prevent someone from visiting the building, again, if they wanted to visit it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I've already mentioned how many guests or representatives I received.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, in the same document that you were shown by the Prosecution, P371, there were a lot of annexes. In annex D of that document, which is a report on inter-ethnic violence in Vitez, Busovaca, and Zenica, in annex D, reference is made to a meeting with Hadzihasanovic, the commander of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH. With regard to access to the music school, this document says the following: "Access to the music school is not problematic, but it is first necessary to make a telephone call." As far as you know, and on the basis of your knowledge of Mr. Hadzihasanovic, could you testify before this Trial Chamber whether Mr. Hadzihasanovic would have provided anyone access to all buildings that belonged to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Objection. That's pure speculation whether he can answer what Mr. Hadzihasanovic would have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this isn't a matter of speculation. I'm reading out a sentence from the Prosecution's document, and General Hadzihasanovic says that access to the music school is not a problem. And since the witness has stated that he knows General Hadzihasanovic, I'm asking him to say whether the general would have always granted such access. It's not a matter of speculation.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Hadzihasanovic would have granted such access. I had contact with him on a number of occasions, and as far as joint cooperation with concerned, and as far as defence of the country is concerned, if he couldn't attend, someone from the 3rd Corps always attended such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, in the document P371, drafted by the humanitarian section of the European monitors, in fact it was drafted by Charles McLeod, there were numerous documents. First there's a report on events and notes on the reports and then there are numerous annexes, one of which has been shown by my learned colleague. I also read out just one sentence from another annex. Since at that time you were the president of the Executive Committee, I would just like to read out something from the report, something that was established in conversation with numerous people. And could you then tell me whether this report reflects the situation in Zenica at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, who would like to raise an objection, Defence counsel would like the witness to say what he thinks about a document drafted by Mr. McLeod. But the slight problem, the minor problem that we have is that he is not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I referred to document P371, a Prosecution document. It could be shown to the witness right now. I could read out the text. It's one page. And this is a document that the Prosecution used a while ago when cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Prosecution. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, the Defence counsel is saying that you have produced a document in the course of your cross-examination of the witness. The document is P371. And Defence counsel, when re-examining the witness, would like to put a question to the witness that is in direct connection with the document. What is the objection you would like to state?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's not technically an objection, but it's a huge document, so before she asks him or including in her question if she could mention the annex, because there are several annexes. So we can have a look at it. And the second point is: Because it's such a big document, having various notes of meetings over time, I don't think it's appropriate just to question him in redirect on all these things, only on issues which I have raised. That would be my objection. So before I know which part of the document she is referring to, I cannot really object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Could you tell us the part of the document that you intend to present, because we read it on several occasions and it's a fairly lengthy document. So which portion of it do you have in mind, do you wish to ask him about?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as I've already stated, this is a lengthy document, P371, which was put before the witness by the Prosecutor, gives me the right to use each portion of that document too. There is a main report, which is to be found at the beginning of the document, and it is one page long. And I'd like to put that main report to the witness, once all the discussions were over, what the international community thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzaferovic, I'm going to read this slowly for the interpretation. It is a report on the events in Vitez and Zenica. The date is April 1993. "After the events in Vitez and Zenica in the second half of April, I went to the region to talk to the leading members of both communities there. My object was to learn what had happened and to convince both sides that they should not allow this to be repeated, whatever the reasons might be for that. Since my report is a fairly lengthy one, I shall briefly present my thoughts on the matter. The day is the 16th of April, and the Croats in Vitez started a continuous attack against the Muslim villages around Vitez and their attack on Stari Vitez, part of the town inhabited by a majority Muslim population."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... fail to see why Defence counsel is reading this document. It's in evidence. It's evidence. And if the witness has something to add to a specific thing which arose out of my cross-examination, I have no problem with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. However, she is reading it, because the witness hasn't got it in front of his eyes. So -- and he will be better able to follow it in his own language. And of course what is being read out is being interpreted. So he will know what the document is about and will be able to give us his opinion of it. Otherwise, we could have just placed the document in front of him, translated in B/C/S. But to save time, and in view of all the other circumstances, you can continue reading the document. Because anyway, it's the Judges who will decide what weight to give to the document. You're going to exchange your arguments, but we shall, of course, draw our own conclusions. Please go ahead, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At the same time, they arrested 13 prominent members of the Muslim community who were also prominent citizens of Vitez. Two of them were killed by firearms while being arrested, two were released, and two still remain in gaol. The strongest attack was the attack on Ahmici when 90 per cent of the Muslim houses were destroyed and more than 100 civilians killed, all -- of which many were burnt in their houses alive. At the same time, the Croats tried to displace the Muslims from Zenica and the surrounding villages in order to justify the expulsion of the Muslims from Vitez. As a result of the propaganda waged and the people in Vitez listened to, many Croats did indeed decide to leave their homes. And most of the Croats returned to their houses in Zenica municipality. There was some destruction of property, but the authorities are working to provide greater security and confidence. The Muslim population in Vitez municipality is now concentrated in Stari Vitez, which resembles a minute version of the Warsaw ghetto, and in Kruscica, a village to the south of Vitez, that is Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond equally cut off.
