The same is true of Busovaca." Mr. President, in view of the objection, I have just read two-thirds of the report. The Court has it in their documents, in their files. So to avoid having fresh arguments put forward in objection, tell me, Mr. Dzaferovic, please:

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are these the facts as you know them from that period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness is allowed to answer, the Prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No word today was uttered, certainly not by me, about the events in Vitez. And I've said before, it's a big document, it's several annexes which have the same author, but aren't linked to each other. I simply don't see why in re-examination whole documents which are already in evidence are read out. And he was the mayor of Zenica, not of Vitez. I simply cannot see the relevance of reading this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead, madam, with respect to relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I already read out the portions relating to Zenica, and this one-page report, which is the main report, does not mention in a single word either the music school or the mistreatment in Zenica or anything else along those lines. And after all, the conversations and discussions that took place, this was the conclusion made by the European observers, and that is what I wanted to tie up with the question that I asked the witness and his testimony. I don't think we need waste more time on that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So that was the conclusion for the witness. But what we would like to know, Witness, is: You've just heard this read out. Do you have any comments to make? And then I'll give the floor to the Prosecution, having heard the witness. Do you have any comments to make on what has just been read out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no comment. It's pure fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. No comments, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now my last question. My colleague showed you a document of the staff of the supreme command by Commander Rasim Delic. Do you know at all in what way a commander of the Main Staff receives his information?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know about the chain of command and how this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you were shown a statement made by your neighbour, Mr. Viskovic, a moment ago, where the security was mentioned and the MOS as well. Did the MOS exist while you were mayor?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I explained at the beginning that all the members of the Bosniak people, whether in the police, the army, or what else, whether they were called Mujahedin or MOS or whatever. Anyway, the Muslim army, Alija's army. There were different terms that they were known by. But that is a notorious lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There's only one matter to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sir, it was put to you by the Prosecution that the ICRC was prevented from visiting the music school, and you replied that you had never heard that before. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Can you confirm from what you knew at the time when you were in Zenica that indeed various international organisations, including the EUMM and the Red Cross, did in fact visit the KP Dom and the music school?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I have already said the circumstances under which I visited the music school, with two secretaries, Brane Ivanovic and the other man accompanying me. So that every meeting with representatives of international organisations, that they insisted and didn't insist upon, I insisted on visiting, but they didn't want that. Finally, I should like to emphasise that when arranging humanitarian aid in the town of Zenica, I would certainly have sanctioned the Red Cross. I wouldn't have allowed food to be centralised and become part of the system for the regulation of humanitarian aid. So it is on that basis that I assess that the Red Cross knew how matters stood in Zenica, the real situation. And I say with full responsibility that all the international organisations present and representatives of international and state and humanitarian missions were able to see for themselves that the town and the Zenica municipality respected the constitutional right of each and every citizen. That is to say that regardless of religion and ethnic affiliation and political options, they were treated the same way. They had the same -- absolutely the same and equal rights. And even Croats, for example, were in a much better position. They had more food that was distributed to them. And another good thing that happened in Zenica was that Caritas held public kitchens, soup kitchens for citizens in Zenica. So I assume that the Red Cross, that is to say, would have sanctioned the work of the municipal government had things like that ever happened in the territory of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Before we continue, if you could just confirm, looking at page 48, line 8, it says in the transcript that: "I would have sanctioned the Red Cross." In light of your answers, is it not the correct interpretation that the Red Cross would have sanctioned that work to take place?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Sanctioned the municipality, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: If I can be more specific, given your general answer. You won't know this, but there was evidence presented before the Trial Chamber that the ICRC did visit persons on occasions. This evidence was given by persons who were in the music school. Would such evidence accord with what you knew at the time about access to prisons in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I really do think that I've answered that question already. That is to say, nobody asked me to do that, so I didn't have any comments made like that from the Red Cross. So what the reports were, I really can't say. But the International Red Cross -- every humanitarian organisation had access to all areas and was secured, enjoyed security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And finally, there has been evidence before the Trial Chamber that members of other international organisations, such as the EUMM, including a Mr. Lars Baggesen, did visit the music school. Once again, would that evidence accord with what your understanding at the time was about access to prisons in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness answered what he knew about this on several occasions. I think he confirmed that. I don't think it's appropriate for the Defence now in re-examination to put to him what other witnesses said and ask him whether that's confirmed or not. That's up to the Trial Chamber to -- or for him in closing argument, to say so many witnesses testified on certain points. He gave his answer. Nothing else, and I think that should be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the practice before this Trial Chamber has been repeatedly to put evidence that previous witnesses gave to current witnesses to test the veracity of that evidence. And I'm simply putting to the witness that there has been previous evidence about access to the music school by the EUMM, and I've mentioned a name Mr. Baggesen. He might know this person. I'm just asking him whether he can confirm that that evidence is correct. Because it would be our submission that that evidence is true, and we wish to determine whether or not this witness can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Just a moment. Stop there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Defence wishes to ask the witness, one, whether he heard about Mr. Baggesen; two, can he confirm from his point of view, that there might have been visitors, international visitors, or others, who were at the music school, because the Defence Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond told us there were people who have come here to testify on several occasions, and we were able to confront different confrontations and documents with the testimony given, either to highlight certain points or to test the credibility of a witness. So it is along those lines that the Defence wishes to ask you the question. Now, the Prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I believe you're right, Mr. President. If Mr. Dixon wants to ask him whether he knew Mr. Baggesen, whether they discussed visits of Mr. Baggesen to the music school, I have no problem. But this is not an expert who is about to get different witness testimonies and makes his conclusions. He is a fact witness. He said what he knows. And Mr. Dixon can inquire further. But to just tell him what other witnesses said I believe is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is what all the parties and Your Honours have indeed been doing throughout the trial, to ask witnesses about what other witnesses have said. In some systems, that is done; in others not. But certainly before the International Tribunal, which has a more flexible system, that is a way of questioning witnesses. And I'm simply wanting to know from him if a witness said I went to visit the music school on a particular day, that was Mr. Baggesen, I had access to the music school, would that seem to be true to him, given what he knew at the time? He was there on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to dwell on individual statements, but I say with full responsibility, having taken the oath before this Honourable Tribunal, that anybody who wanted to could have gone there, anyone, which means citizens too. On one occasion, when I was a guest at one of the local stations, there were comments and objections made of that kind. And as the president of the Executive Board or member of the local government said: Let's see. Let's test the situation. And we can go and visit it. So I say with full responsibility before this Honourable Tribunal, having taken the solemn declaration, that anybody could have visited the music school if they had wanted to. And as for other statements, I really can't say whether they were ill intentioned or well-intentioned or why they were given, for what reason. I can't say. But I repeat once again before this Honourable Court that I say with full responsibility, and I have taken the oath to tell the truth, that anybody could have visited the music school, anybody who wanted to. Without going in to enumerate other ethnic groups who went to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as I'm concerned, I just have a few small questions to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to say that as far as we're concerned, you're not a second-rate citizen, second-class citizen. You have, of course, taken the solemn oath to speak the truth, and so we consider that you are doing so. And your past situation will have nothing to do with our own appreciation of your testimony. The Defence showed you a document a moment ago, a book, in fact, written by Mr. Spahic, who was the president of the War Presidency. My question for you is this: Have you read the book?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Partially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you read it partially.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I say "partially" because I was an eyewitness to the events, so I know of all the events that he's writing about. It happened while I was president of the municipal government myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So in that book, on page 112, the author of the document relates a conversation that he had with Mr. Lebourg, which the name doesn't tell me anything. Mr. Lebourg. Do you know who Mr. Lebourg is? Because his name is cited in the document. No? It doesn't ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who the president of the municipality had talks with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, anyway, in the document, they discuss the subject of Mujahedins, and my question to you is based on the document and follows on from it. As far as you're concerned - you yourself lived in Zenica - did you see any Mujahedin yourself?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to Mujahedin, that is to say, foreign citizens staying -- residing in the area of Zenica, I just had one meeting with two representatives. They were wearing white robes and came to me asking for assistance, that is to say, logistical support, in terms of food. I sent them to the 3rd Corps, referred them to the 3rd Corps, and said that it was only by decision and request of the 3rd Corps that we could do anything about that and ensure food supplies. That was the only time I met any one of them. But we did take measures, take steps to establish the identity of these people, and we insisted upon checking out their papers, and asked the Ministry of the Interior to do, so especially since there was an incident that took place in Zenica in which two humanitarian workers were killed, I think. And the people -- the perpetrators were brought to task, sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that in Zenica there were about 40 humanitarian organisations and that you dealt with the question of refugees, food, et cetera. Now, we have also been told, because a number of witnesses came in here, and we were told that those foreigners had come to bring aid in food and to support the people, assist the people, in terms of money, food, different types of aid. In your capacity, and with your responsibilities, did you have any knowledge of that aid that was mentioned, and was it effective in helping out the refugees?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: You mean the Mujahedin? Is that what you're referring to? Well, I really didn't know about that aid and assistance. The humanitarian organisations that we communicated with, and they have been recorded, I believe, in the secretariat for the economy, and of course the Ministry of the Interior, I assume, recorded the existence of these 40-odd humanitarian organisations. The UNHCR can be highlighted in particular. Now, had that organisation, if it had worked under any name, I wasn't aware of it. And I assume that it did not have any major effect in the sense of humanitarian aid or food aid. So I say with full responsibility that the municipality reaped no benefit from any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Spahic says in his book, and that is on page 14 of the translation - I'm reading page 14 - he says that their "humanitarian activity was negligible." He also says that, that it was negligible. What do you think, that humanitarian activity was negligible, he says?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I say that too. Any contribution in material terms or food or anything like that, I wasn't aware are, actually. I can't remember. Of course, I can't remember all the organisations, but I'm sure if you look at the archives you could look at the names of the different organisations. We had joint meetings several times a week, because this was warranted by the events on the ground, what was going on in that period of time, meant that we had to have frequent meetings. So I had contacts, very good contacts, with those organisations working in the Zenica area. But the meetings were usually presided over by the representative of the UNHCR. In the first -- my first half of my mandate, it was Mr. de la Mota, and afterwards it was the other man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of your testimony - and I'm relying on my memory - you speak about organisations and you brought up the name of Merhamet, an organisation called Merhamet. Could you tell us a little more about that organisation, which was a charity organisation?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I can compare Merhamet, it's the same as Caritas, a charity organisation. Rather, these were the ones I knew, and they took part in that kind of work. So -- and the translation of the name itself, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Merhamet, means to be good, to be nice, to look nice, to respect others, and so on. That's the translation of the word "Merhamet" itself, which is what the organisation goes by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you have any meetings with the responsible people from that organisation? And if so, do you happen to remember a name, one of the names?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: You mean of the Merhamet organisation? Is that what you mean? Well, they were representatives, but I can't remember their names, but they were people from the local area, from Zenica, and they were organised up to state level. They were organisations which were active in the municipality and in the district but I can't remember any specific names now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the composition of that organisation, its members, according to you, were people -- were nationals, locals. There wasn't -- there weren't any foreigners in the Merhamet organisation?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly not. The headquarters were in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another question relating to financial matters, because you have an understanding of finances, you're an auditor, and I assume that your municipality had some financial problems because you had to find food and so on. Did you have a way of funding, of financing this, apart from the funds you received from the state? Were there any private donations made by private individuals or coming in from abroad, for example? Can you tell us about that, be more specific, how this was financed, this humanitarian work?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: So on the question of financing the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the local authorities were duty-bound to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm not talking about the financing of the army. I just mean the money you needed, the funds you needed in your municipal activity to go about your business, which might have come from private donations, private individuals, companies, associations, things like that.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: No. Not a single BH dinar or convertible German mark, as it was known - that was the method of payment, the currency at the time. Not a single mark, and I say that with full responsibility, came into the municipal budget, except the decision made by the Presidency of the Zenica municipality, and confirmed by parliament, and in keeping with the provision and law on the -- governing the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the burden of the war should be equally distributed amongst the economy. So that was the only source of financing. And credits that were given by the investment and commercial bank of Zenica, the loans they gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I have one or two questions on the music school that has been discussed several times. I take it, but please correct me, that the music school is owned by the municipality of Zenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That is to say, the school centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with the army in 1993. Was it requisitioned by the army or was it given to the army? What was the relationship between the army and the civil authorities, as far as the music school is concerned?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Up until June 1993, when I arrived on the scene, there was a secretariat for defence, which had to report to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it had the Executive Committee above it. It had to report on materiel and technical equipment. And this building was mobilised by the secretariat for defence for Zenica municipality. And that was the case for many other buildings and other equipment. And this was in accordance with the law on the armed forces. It was done illegally [as interpreted], in accordance with the regulations that were in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My question is the following: Would you be authorised, as being the presidents of the War Presidency, to order visitors -- to order the army to accept visitors of the building?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I'll just have to correct you. I wasn't the president of the Presidency. I was the president of the local municipal government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, then let me say in your capacity in 1993. Would you be authorised to tell the army to let visitors, international visitors or humanitarian visitors, visit the building?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Why not? If we respected the principle of divided responsibilities, it would -- if you bear in mind the responsibilities that the army had, there was the HVO, the ABiH, the Ministry of the Interior. But there was coordination, and there was such coordination on the basis of the law. If a commander said it was necessary to have a visit, I think that that request would not have been complied with [as interpreted]. That's what I think. I don't know if I've been sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, that's my question, really. I don't know what the relationship between the civil authorities and the military authorities are -- were at the time in 1993. But if I were an army man, and I used building by the civil authorities, I would perhaps have the feeling that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Mr. Bourgon. A translation problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in fact, Mr. President. In the witness's last answer, page 58, when he answered the question, it says: "I think that that request would have been complied with." But the transcript says "would not have been complied with." Perhaps Judge Swart could put the question to the witness again, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let me ask the question again, because I have some difficulty in understanding the question. So my question was: If some visitors came to you and asked for permission to visit the music school, which was in use by the military, could you authorise the military, the commander, the local commander of the school, to accept the visit of an observer, international or other observer?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he could have called me, but this would have been done through the 3rd Corps. If a visit was involved. I couldn't directly participate in this. The division of responsibilities was respected during that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the Judges have put their questions to the witness and the witness has answered the questions, both parties have the right to put additional questions to the witness in order to clarify certain answers or to obtain additional information. But I will first ask the Prosecution whether they have any additional questions, and afterwards the Defence may take the floor. Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just one small issue, Mr. Dzaferovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In answer to one of Their Honour's questions, you said that -- you mentioned an incident in Zenica when I believe two humanitarian workers were wounded or killed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you continued saying that "the perpetrators were brought to sanctions." Now, tell me first: Who, according to your information, were the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, at a meeting held on the following day - this took place in the evening - a meeting was held, a security meeting, attended by representatives of the authorities and of the judiciary, and we were informed that the man who had allegedly perpetrated the crime was in detention. And that is all the information I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The context of the question you were asked was about, I believe, foreign people, Mujahedin. So I just ask to clarify --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that the Mujahedin were in question. I mentioned two humanitarian workers who had been killed. And I said that the person who had perpetrated the crime had been arrested. He was in detention. And the president of the high court, Mr. Djuro Goblak, informed us of this, in the presence of about 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But what do you know about the perpetrator, if anything? Was he a Muslim, a Croat? Was he a soldier, was he a civilian? If you know.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the municipal government. This was the task of the security services centre. It wasn't my task. And as I respect the principle of the division of responsibilities, it wasn't my right to request any information or to obtain any information. And you know that this involved organs of prosecution and investigation at the time, who were responsible for taking the appropriate measures within the framework of court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you don't know who the perpetrator was, civilian, soldier, policeman?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No questions any more, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Defence counsel who called the witness may now put additional questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzaferovic, it seems to me you mentioned which organisation those two individuals belonged to, those two individuals who were killed. But I'm not sure it's been entered into the transcript. Could you mention the name.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: The humanitarian organisation called Oda.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I only have one more question in relation to a question put to you by one of the Judges. You said what you would have done if someone had requested access to the music school. Since you're so open to suggestions, comments made by citizens, because you mentioned 5.600 individuals, who visited you, tell me whether at any point in time any of the citizens, and of the any of the humanitarian or religious organisations or anyone else, did anyone ever come to complain to you about the fact that a military unit, a brigade or a corps, had refused them access to the music school. Did anyone ever complain to you about this?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: No. On the contrary. Perhaps I failed to mention to the Chamber that in my office, Father Radic was present on a daily basis, as well as the late Drincic. We dealt with common problems, and there were certain incidents in Zenica. There were 82 local communes in the municipality of Zenica. And as the president, and with my vice-president, Zelko Tadic, and Father Radic, we would visit villages were the majority of the population were Croats. Those villages were Gornja Zenica, Janjac, Cajdras, et cetera, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my very final question, since you have mentioned the name of your vice-president on a number of occasions, Mr. Tadic. What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DZAFEROVIC
utterances.text: He was a Croat, and he became the vice-president of the Executive Committee representing the HDZ, and his president was Josip Pojavnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, sir. This concludes your testimony. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for having come to testify in The Hague. We wish you all the best. We wish you a good trip home. And naturally, as the new year has just commenced, we wish you all the best in your career. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to the Defence to inform us of the second witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would first like to suggest that the documents on our list of documents from 1 to 7 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will deal with that. Very well. Defence counsel is requesting that the documents recognised by the witness be admitted into evidence, documents that he had signed, a book that he recognised and that he had read. What is the Prosecution's position with regard to these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes. The book, obviously, it's been authored by somebody else, and -- but we believe it's up to Your Honours to decide which weight to give to such a hearsay document. We have no objections to tendering it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In fact, the Chamber shall assess the weight to be given to the documents. Mr. Registrar, could we have exhibit numbers for the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have a list of seven documents. The first one, the official journal, number 2/93, shall be admitted into evidence. The number will be DH1985 and the English version DH1985/E. This is the gazette. The second document, dated the 31st of May, 1993, shall be admitted into evidence. The number will be DH1986. And the English version shall be DH1986/E. The third document, dated the 4th of June, 1993, the number -- the local number, internal number 025371/93. This document shall be admitted into evidence, and the number will be DH1987. The English version will be DH1987/E. The fourth document, dated the 4th of June, 1993, has an internal number which is 025372/93. It shall be admitted into evidence and the number will be DH1988. The English version will be DH1988/E. The fifth document is dated the 7th of June, 1993, and it will be admitted into evidence. The number will be DH1989. The number of the English version will be DH1989/E. The sixth document is dated the 8th of June, 1993. It shall be admitted into evidence and the number will be DH1990. The English version will be DH1990/E. And finally, the seventh document is a document that was marked for identification and will now be given the definitive exhibit number, DH1593. And the English version will be DH1593/E. I have now dealt with all the documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, please say that you can hear and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you please tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Hamdija Kulovic. I was born on the 6th of February, 1948, in Zenica, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you currently employed? And if so, what position do you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am currently employed in an agency for privatisation in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are a functionary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work for the agency for privatisation. It's not a state service. It's a specialised organisation that is involved in privatising selected companies within the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In 1992 and 1993, over ten years ago, did you hold a position of any kind? What did you do at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until 1992, I was the director of the largest steel plant in Zenica. That company had 23.000 workers and it produced over 2 million tonnes and 2 billion dollars was its annual revenue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, I was the general director of the entire plant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before a national or international court about the events that took place in your country in 1992 or 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today will be the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. You will now have to answer the questions that will be put to you by Defence counsel, who are to your left. You have certainly had the opportunity of meeting them when you were proofed for this hearing. Once this stage has been completed, I'm not sure how long it will last for the moment, but once this stage has been completed, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will commence with their cross-examination. After they have concluded their cross-examination, they'll have the same amount of time as the Defence. After that stage, the Defence counsel can put additional questions to you that are related to questions that are put to you by the Prosecution. The three Judges sitting before you may then ask you questions in order to clarify some of your answers or for any other reasons, and in the interest of justice. Once the Judges have put their questions to you, the Prosecution and the Defence, who will take the floor last, may ask you additional questions. And that is when we will have completed your testimony. I don't know whether this will be completed today or tomorrow, or rather, on Monday. But if we're not able to finish with your testimony today, you'll have to continue on Monday. As you have taken the solemn declaration, you should not give false testimony, but I assume that you are aware of the fact. In addition, I would like to point out something that shouldn't be applicable to you. If a witness believes that an answer he provides might be used against him at a subsequent date, the witness may refuse to answer the question. In such a case, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question. In such exceptional circumstances, and we have never been faced with such a situation to date, in such exceptional circumstances, the Chamber grants the witness a form of immunity. If you find the question is complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. Be aware of the fact that your testimony is very important because we have no written documents that concern you. We know nothing about you. This is why your oral testimony is so important. Roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding. We have about another ten minutes before the break. I don't know whether Defence counsel would like to start their examination-in-chief now or after the break. It's for the Defence to decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think we could start now. And could the usher distribute a bundle of documents to the witness, the Chamber, and my learned colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Kulovic. While these documents are being distributed, there is something else I would like to point out to you, Mr. Kulovic. As we speak the same language, you might want to answer my question as soon as I have put it to you. But since it's important to interpret my questions and your answers so that everyone in the courtroom can follow our, exchange, I would be grateful if you would leave a brief pause after I have put my question to you. Have you understood what I'm saying? Have you understood what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were the director of the steelworks plant, and then you were the general director of the entire steel plant. Tell me something about your educational background. What are you by profession and where were you educated?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I'm an engineer in metallurgy and I completed my education, primary school, secondary school, and the university, in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In April 1992, what post did you occupy?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: In April 1992 I was the director of the biggest part of the Zenica steelworks, which had 6.000 workers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulovic, at any point in time, did you also have a military function to perform, in addition to your professional duties?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Up until April 1992, or by April 1992, I had completed my military service, which lasts for one year. That was sometime in 1973. And when I served in the military, I completed the school for reserve officers. My specialty was the construction of roads, bridges, so it concerned engineering work and units involving engineering. This was up until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: There was a decision - I don't know the exact date - a company decision, and the Ironworks Battalion, the so-called Ironworks Battalion was formed. There were 1.300 men in it. It was based in the company. It wasn't armed, nor did it have any military characteristics. The men would only gather occasionally in order to protect the property of the company, the men in the company, et cetera. When the municipal authorities spoke to the commander of the garrison of the JNA in Zenica, well, these discussions ran into a crisis, and a different team of people continued with these discussions. On behalf of the JNA, General Sipcic came to Zenica. He was a general who was in charge of withdrawing the JNA from Slovenia, and he was very successful in completing this task. And on behalf of the BH authorities, three civilians were responsible for these discussions: I, as the commander of that unarmed battalion; Mr. Mirsad Mesic, who was the commander of the municipal staff of civilian protection; and Mr. Branko Boncina, the commander of the municipal staff of People's Defence. After a few days of discussions, we had agreed on certain details on how JNA units were to withdraw. This task was completed very successfully and there were not even minor incidents. The task was carried out by men from the Zenica Ironworks Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the fact that you were the commander of the Ironworks Battalion. Tell me: Up until when were you the commander of the Ironworks Battalion, and afterwards, were you only involved in business or did you have a military position of any kind?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I remained the commander of the Ironworks Battalion until the beginning of July. So for about two months after the barracks was taken over. I was then appointed as the general director of the company, and I remained in that position until the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kulovic. Mr. Kulovic, could you please tell me, as a prominent businessman in Zenica, as a prominent citizen of Zenica: Do you know what sort of units, for the purpose of defending the country, were created in Zenica in the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do know that war is a serious matter and can't be left to chance. You can't tolerate wilful behaviour in such a situation. And I quickly came to realise that order in society, cracking down on crime and paramilitary formations, et cetera, was a key issue if the state was to survive. I frequently spoke to members of the international community who were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they were of the same opinion. They believed that dealing with such issues was of crucial importance for the survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'll now describe the actual situation that prevailed in Zenica at the time. It was -- it became very chaotic very rapidly. The situation deteriorated very rapidly. In just one month, in May and June and July, schools of units were formed in Zenica, units that had very differing ideologies and very different insignia, different characteristics. They were formed by individuals problematic individuals in Zenica at the time. They were also formed by politicians, and there were even units that were formed by Zenica businessmen, people who had money and who would form a unit consisting of 50 or a hundred men. They would train it, finance it, and place themselves at the head of these units. At that time, there were a number of units that had been formed by the municipal staff, and the Ironworks Battalion was one of those units. And there were two other battalions that were subsequently formed by Ironworks employees. In addition, there was a HOS unit. This was a party unit. It belonged to the Croatian Peasants Party. There was an HVO unit which was an HDZ party unit. And a few months earlier on, there was the so-called Patriotic League. There was the Green League, that consisted of about 70 men. I don't know who formed this unit. Muslim forces soon appeared as well, guerrilla forces appeared, and there were private armies, as I have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It would perhaps be a good time to have a break now, Mr. President, and I will continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is now half past 12.00. We will have our technical break and we will resume at about 5 to 1.00, and we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we perhaps just have a 15- or 20-minute break to try and conclude the examination of this witness today? Thank you. Perhaps you could bear this request in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll reduce the break to 15 minutes. So we will resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulovic, just before the break you were explaining to us what the situation was like in Zenica in 1992. Tell me now, please: Do you happen to know whether at some point in time toward the end of 1992, Enver Hadzihasanovic arrived with the aim of forming a corps? Do you know about that fact? Were you aware of that, its flow? Tell me about the problems he encountered were.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of 1992 he did come to Zenica, probably with the task of putting law and order into the chaotic state that reigned in the town, that is to say, Commander Hadzihasanovic arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to take a look at documents 1 and 2 that are in front of you and that I gave you during our preparations for testimony. Take a look at them, please, and tell us whether these two documents compiled by Commander Hadzihasanovic, one in November 1992 and one in February 1993, whether they reflect the situation as it was during that period of time in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I think that these documents --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer. Do they or do they not?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: A large number of units that were formed with different ideologies and different sources of supplies, with different interests, mostly personal interests, made the situation in town for normal people inexplicable. Every third man was wearing a uniform, for example, in town, and had -- and publicly displayed weapons. Units would come to companies, without any documents, any papers whatsoever, or with invalid documents, would seize cars, for example, and other property belonging to the company or enterprise, or they would take over space in the firm, the premises. And the management of the firm had to move out, and they would move in to those premises. And all the important premises, starting out with hotels, for example, important buildings, hotels, the student cultural centre, school buildings, old-age pensioners' homes and things like that, they were taken over by the military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulovic, what you're just saying now, do you -- let me just clarify matters. Do you want to say that the situation was more difficult than it was as stipulated in the documents written by Commander Hadzihasanovic which he encountered when he came to form the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. So the situation was much more difficult. He was there for just a brief period of time and wasn't able to assess the situation fully. But I, as a citizen of Zenica myself, as an inhabitant, was fully conscious of the gravity of the situation that prevailed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As somebody working in the economy and as a resident, after Commander Hadzihasanovic came and established the 3rd Corps, soon after that, were you able to notice any changes or changes in the way in which the situation was dealt with, the chaos was dealt with?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: As the director of a large company who had very good men working for me, the workers and employees of the Zenica ironworks, I was able to protect the company's property. And on the compound of the ironworks, which was larger than the town, in fact, 4 million square metres, not a single unit entered that space that took over the compound. But that was at great risk, because I was constantly open to pressure and violent pressure to have somebody seize something from the enterprise, from storming the premises and taking over property. There were even demands that that part of town where the company was should be handed over to a unit to control. Other companies weren't in a situation like that. When Mr. Hadzihasanovic arrived, I received confirmation that everything that did not come from any official command of the units should be taken account of. And without official papers, I was not to meet anybody's demands or comply with anybody's demands, unless they had the necessary official papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We heard here that the command of the 3rd Corps was located in one of the buildings belonging to the Zenica ironworks. Could you tell me, please, whether, with your personal example of the relationship to what the command needed, did Commander Hadzihasanovic try and bring law and order back to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the corps command really did take up the premises one metre [as interpreted] from the main headquarters building, in a premises there. It was the building of our project bureaus, our design offices. And in order to cut our costs for heating and to rationalise the heating, we moved to the main building, and that building was left empty. The building we were in previously was left empty. There was a mistake made by the director of the project bureau. Before Mr. Hadzihasanovic arrived, somebody else had taken over the premises, that is to say, soldiers, without the necessary authorisation and papers. But when Mr. Hadzihasanovic arrived, we were able to regulate the matter. In keeping with the rules and regulations, the building was mobilised, or requisitioned, and that was in keeping with the law. And from that time on, the company would send out invoices to the army for all the expenses incurred during that particular month.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record: On page 74, line 11, it says that this was one metre away from the main headquarters building, whereas the witness said 100 metres. So the figure is 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The project bureau was opposite the other side of the road and it was about a hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulovic, tell me, please: Were you witness of the difficult situation that reigned between those individual groups, and how difficult was it to establish law and order, and what did Mr. Hadzihasanovic have to encounter? What resistance did he encounter from these numerous groups, and how hard was it for him to discipline them?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the very beginning, I was quite clear that the mission assigned to Commander Hadzihasanovic was no easy mission. It was not at all easy to carry it out. I'm a practical man myself, but I considered that the task was well-nigh impossible. The decision to introduce law and order was brought in too late to begin with, and that it would be very difficult, and I thought that it would be almost impossible to introduce law and order properly. After this decision was taken for individual units formed in the way they were formed, should be attached to the -- or come under the supervision of the corps command by means of forming brigades, I attended a meeting of the commanders of the Patriotic League, for example, and Mr. Hadzihasanovic. That wasn't the worst unit with the most problems, but it was interesting to see how much effort had to be invested in remaining outside the brigade command and corps command. They did what they could. They made promises about thousands of soldiers, of asking for less supplies, whereas in fact I felt that what they were really trying to do was to remain outside the system of command and outside the authority of the command, that they would like to stay in town and to play it being combatants, whereas they weren't really combatants or fighters. They wanted to have their own logistics, and probably to further their own interests of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulovic, you said that the intention was to have law and order prevail. Tell me, please: Was it precisely Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic who, throughout 1993, was the head of that principle, that there must be law and order in the army?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. He was guided by that principle, and all his attentions were spent trying to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, please, Mr. Kulovic -- or rather, take a look at document number 3 first, please, and read the last sentence of paragraph 1 of that document. But before you do so, let me ask you: Your steelworks, ironworks, was the R.N.K. So it was the mine and ironworks of Zenica. Is that right? And you knew the situation in the mine and the ironworks from the position you occupied?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: This is document 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you first: Were you fully abreast of the situation in the mines and the ironworks?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew of all the details, the entire situation. I'm an inhabitant of Zenica myself. I knew thousands of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, let's have a look at document 3, and the number is P655 [as interpreted]. Would you read out paragraph -- the last sentence of paragraph 1, beginning with the words "towards the Croats."

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I can't find the beginning, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "The Muslim party behaves towards the Croats in Zenica as if they were slaves, because they are under physical pressure and forced to work in the mines, to join the Muslim army. They are subject to threats. Their family is subject to threats," and so on. Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since you are a citizen of Zenica yourself and was the managing director, did this ever happen during the war in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't wish to deny that there were individual crimes committed in Zenica and that members of all three ethnic groups suffered at the hands of wilful people, madmen wearing uniforms, but I would like to say that I don't agree with the way this was stated. I was the director of a large company from 1992 onwards, and my secretary was a Croatian lady. She was a Croat from Bosnia. And my driver was a Bosnian Serb, for example. Two of my four advisors, two were Bosnian Serbs. Of the 15 or so managing directors, six directors of various plants, or rather, seven, managers were either Bosnian Croats or Bosnian Serbs, for example. And I know about a large number of people in Zenica, of a large number of people in Zenica, who lived in great harmony together in these difficult times. But I don't wish to deny, having said that, that there were excessive situations, there were killings, unjustified, arbitrary killings, brutal killings. But this description does not correspond to the situation as it was. I want to say that it was wartime, and I myself was jeopardised at the time. I felt myself to be very insecure and unsafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me: In view of the fact that you say that it was absolutely incorrect that they were slaves or taken to the mines, et cetera, et cetera, were you ever faced at that time with a concept, a general concept of terrible propaganda that was unleashed in Zenica, which depicted the situation in a quite distorted manner, different from what you described it, that it was a state of war with excessive situations, but not in the way it was described by HVO propaganda, for instance?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew the importance of propaganda, given the conditions that prevailed, but I could never have imagined that propaganda could go to such lengths and have such terrible consequences and that it could be used and wielded in that way. So, on the one hand, I was proclaimed a traitor by my own people, as somebody who helped others, and the Croatian people, the -- or rather, the HVO, issued an order that I should be arrested at a checkpoint as being some kind of protagonist of the idea and concept of a Muslim state, which of course was not true. I remember several cases in point. For example, there were writings in some Serb papers, that in the Zenica ironworks, in the furnace, people were being burnt alive, for example. That was one form of propaganda which was just nonsensical. And it was just nonsense. And towards the end of the war, representatives of the international forces came to see me to ask about information concerning people who had allegedly been incarcerated in the ironworks and were doing forced labour there, which of course was not true at all. We had about 5.000 people working there, and we managed to get through the war without a single incident. And I think that amongst the workers themselves there was not a single argument that broke out, in fact, not a single brawl. And I remember one detail particularly well, and that was when there was a ceremony in Zenica that we organised. The ceremonial unveiling of the statue of the Virgin Mary. We had helped have the monument erected. All the people of Zenica gathered at the ceremony, and a small incident did take place there, when all the people were rallied in front of the church, in the church itself, and so on. What happened was that a jeep turned up with armed soldiers who fired several bullets into the air. Nobody paid any particular attention to that, although normal people didn't like seeing this happening. But several days after that, my deputy called me, and after the BH army and HVO conflicts had begun, he remained cut off in the Republic of Croatia. He was in Croatia at the time. And we just had 11 people who were not in Zenica. They were on business trips in Croatia, Italy, Austria, or wherever, and they were cut off from Zenica. As we just had one mobile phone connection with the outside world, he phoned me up and asked me what had happened at the church of St. Ilijas. And I said that nothing special had happened, that I was there, that I stood there with the Croats of Zenica, and with Predrag Andjelovic and some other people and that everything passed by quite normally just for that one small incident. He said that when he heard about it, it affected him very adversely and that he was crying all the time and that the news bulletin said that 16 or 17 Croats had been hanged to death in front of the church. So there you see what the strength that propaganda had and what it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now look at document 4.2, paragraph 2 of document 4. The number is 1423. And tell me whether you recognise this type of propaganda that was to do more than weapons were able to do during the war.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think this was aimed at having the Croats move from where they had been living until then. And we're talking about 1993, I think, almost towards the end of the conflict between the army and the HVO, when the situation came to a head, and this was designed to aggravate the situation. And I have never been able to understand why people did things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago, Mr. Kulovic, that you were there with Friar Petar Andjelovic, who was the provincial priest, and that you were there with other priests. But tell us your relationship to the -- with the Croats in Zenica generally speaking. Did you have personal friends among the Croats of Zenica, or rather, did you socialise with the brethren, Catholic brethren in Zenica, Catholic priests in Zenica during 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: My relationship generally towards members of the church, whether they be Catholics or Orthodox or whatever, and of course the Islamic religious community, was a very special relationship. If we would attend joint meetings, for example, or talks, then all three drove in the car there with me. As far as Brother Stipan is concerned, Friar Stipan, I had a particular friendship with him, and the fires of the Church of St. Mark's are of the Franciscan order and they always came out in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina and life in common. And I think -- at least I heard from certain people that that is why his positions were a little precarious and seen as precarious by part of the Croatian community. We were regular guests, let me tell you, at their church, and we used all opportunities we had to be together with them, to show them, to demonstrate our affiliation to them, and very often we would organise concerts of the philharmonic orchestra in the church or the choir. And as I say, I was on very friendly terms with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulovic, you started off by telling us how you succeeded in dislocating the Yugoslav People's Army from the barracks in Zenica and you mentioned the name of Mr. Mesic, who was commander of the civilian protection unit. Can you tell us, please, whether you are on close terms with Mr. Mesic, and is Mesic one of the people who had constant contact with the Croatian population, and especially with Catholic priests, and a friendly relationship with them in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mesic and I, Mr. Mesic and I are joined by ties of kumship, and I think that our relationship was positive. We did what we could, as far as circumstances permitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In Zenica, do you know whether any friars from the church in Brajkovici ever came?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When there was an open conflict between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina - I don't know how and in what way - but all the priests from Brajkovici, Guca Gora, and so on did come to the St. Mark's church in Zenica. There were three other Catholic churches there, but we came across those friars all in the St. Mark's church.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We have heard testimony before this court by Mr. Mesic, and he said that he brought those friars from Brajkovici there personally. Do you know anything about that? Have you ever heard -- did you ever hear that they were arrested in any way or taken into custody from Brajkovici and Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the St. Mark's church at least 20 or 30 times during that period of time, and what happened, of course, was not a good thing. And we discussed it in a very reasonable way. It was something that was out of our hands. But I never heard of or had knowledge of them having been mistreated in any way or taken into custody or taken prisoner or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in view of the personal positions you occupied and your friendship, tell me, please, whether Friar Stipan Radic or the other friars ever told you of anything that could have presented a major problem in Zenica, such as well-known fact, for example, that the Croats were being taken off to the music school and mistreated there. Did Friar Stipan Radic ever tell you anything like that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Those of us who associated with the friars, and if I can say, the intellectuals of Zenica, we held identical viewpoints on the war and we would talk about the events that took place, and we always had identical viewpoints on current events. I heard rumours going round about people being incarcerated in the music school, but the building is in the centre of town. Of course, I don't exclude the fact that there were people incarcerated in that building. Before Mr. Hadzihasanovic arrived, in fact, some people complained to me, Bosnian Croats or Bosnian Serbs, would come to me and complain that they had been taken off for interrogation. Because the commanders of some of the units, or people who were in charge of security, tried to play at war, I would say, in that way. They tried to intimidate people, people who they thought had money. So things like that did happen in Zenica. Now, I heard rumours about the music school, but let me say probably there were people incarcerated there. But that they were mistreated there, that they were killed, that there were a lot of them incarcerated there, I really can't confirm that. Because the building was small anyway. It was located in the centre of town. And had there been anything like that going on, I think I would have heard about it, because people from there contacted me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody come to you to ask you to do something?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A Croat from Kakanj came to tell me about it. He didn't ask me for my help in any way. But I know the man from before the war. He supplied the mine with some of the technical resources we needed, and we were in contact at the beginning of the war. He said he had been held in the music school for some ten days and that he was released after that. A month later, he opened a petrol station in Kakanj. But he didn't tell me that there had been any mistreatment or abuse of any kind. I don't want to hide any facts from this Court, but he did not tell me that there were any problems. I learnt about things later on. I believe the man. I'm sure he was incarcerated there, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: We heard testimony from Vlado Adamovic before this Court. Had the people had these large-scale problems being taken off to the music school and being mistreated, who would they have contacted for assistance? Would they have contacted you, come to see you, or come to see a judge, for example?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm quite certain that since half the population was linked in one way or another to the ironworks, of the 23.000 employees, 80.000 more were family members, for example. They had great confidence in me, and I think they would come to me first rather than go to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kulovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution. I would like to greet you, Ms. Benjamin. We haven't seen you for a long time. And I'll give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Tecla Henry-Benjamin and I am, along with my colleague, representing the Prosecution in this matter. I have just a few questions for you, and if at any moment you don't understand what I'm saying or you'd like me to repeat the question, feel free to do so and I'll oblige. Thank you. We did go very fast, so I'll try to see how I can keep up. First, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you please explain your position as of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Around the beginning of July, at that time, I was already the director of the entire Zenica ironworks. If you're interested in the situation up to that date, I could explain the situation to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I would just give you the questions and hopefully we'll get the answers. Prior to July of 1992 - and correct me if I'm wrong - were you the commander of the Ironworks Battalion for simply two months?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. For one month we were a unit without any arms. The unit was used to take over the barracks, to take charge of the barracks. Afterwards, the unit was armed, and under the command of the regional staff, it was used in combat activity in Zenica. The combat was in Visoko after that, and I was demobilised. And as this was necessary for the company, I returned to the company.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So would I be correct in saying that your life in the military was rather short-lived?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: By the time General Hadzihasanovic had come to Zenica you were not a member of the military; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but since the corps command was in the vicinity, I had daily contact both with Mr. Hadzihasanovic and with the other subsequent commanders of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know a battalion by the name of Zeljezara?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: That's the battalion that was formed in April 1992, the battalion that had no arms for a month and it was then used as a military unit for a month. And I was then demobilised and returned to the company, where I became its head. The unit continued to exist within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the beginning of 1993, January 1993, and more specifically so, the 26th of January, 1993, could you please state for the Trial Chamber what was the situation in Zenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: That was a period during which the freely formed units in 1992 -- well, we tried to place these units under the corps command. I don't believe that this was fully successful. In the case of certain units they managed to maintain a significant element of independence and they were fiercely resistant to the idea of being placed under a single command. I would also like to point out that in the case of some units, they weren't placed under the corps command, right up until the end of the war. Some units found very bizarre reasons for not cooperating.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think you probably misunderstood the question. My question was: Could you describe for us, from the beginning of January 1993, January, and more specific, around the end, the 26th of January, 1993, what was the prevailing situation, what was the condition in Zenica? What was the atmosphere like?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: There were still a lot of units in Zenica that hadn't become part of the corps. There were conflicts between the ABiH and the HVO, and these conflicts were becoming more frequent. I don't really understand why you're asking me about the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you, because I think you indicated to the Trial Chamber that you were familiar with the Zenica area and what transpired in Zenica. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: If I were to say to you that the Prosecution alleges that there was physical abuse and psychological abuse in Zenica in 1993, and in particular, the Zenica music school, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I would agree that there were individual cases of torture, of violence, but I would not agree that this involved large groups of people. I wouldn't agree that this was something that was done in an organised manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say that Dusina is located in the Zenica municipality? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Dusina is in the municipality of Busovaca, but that's not important. It's in the vicinity of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So I'll accept that. It's in the vicinity of Zenica. And being familiar with the Zenica area and Dusina being in the vicinity of Zenica, could you please indicate to the Trial Chamber as much as you know, only what you know, if anything at all transpired in Dusina in January of 1993. And that is why earlier on I said to you specifically around the 26th, to sort of zero in.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I don't know all the details, but I have heard stories that I don't doubt, stories according to which six Croats, six civilians who were killed in the course of combat operations, and I also heard that people had been tortured, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So you agree with me if I said all was not well in Zenica in January of 1993 and thereafter? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I can't dispute that. I wasn't an eyewitness. I have to accept that those are things that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And I would ask you further: Would you agree with me when I say that not only were you not an eyewitness, as you said, but also you were not a member of any military body during that time? Correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I wasn't a member of any military formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Who, in your opinion, then, would you say was responsible for the events that transpired in Dusina, in Zenica, in January of 1993 and thereafter? Who, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that Defence counsel would be rising to its feet. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't see how the answer Mr. Kulovic provided -- well, given the answer that Mr. Kulovic provided, he said that he wasn't a member of any military formation, I don't see how Mr. Kulovic could answer this question as to who was responsible for those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, given the fact that the witness himself said that he was very familiar with the Zenica area, that he met with the general and he was very familiar with what was going on, I think it's a very appropriate question. I take it, since the Trial Chamber has not objected, I will ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Who, in your opinion, at that time was responsible for the conflict and the prevailing situation that went on in Zenica as of January 1993 and thereon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. You said that you weren't a member of the army at the time, but you are very familiar with the situation in Zenica. This question is really a borderline question, because it's not directly related to what was said a while ago. But as you're a prominent citizen of Zenica, did you have any knowledge about what had happened in Dusina? Did you hear anything about it? What were you told about it? Or do you not know anything about these events? Since you had thousands of people working under you, perhaps you heard about something. This seems to be what the Prosecution is implying. But could you answer the question, in the interest of justice. We have to decide on the issue of Dusina. What could you tell us about this? If you know nothing, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I heard several stories from various sources about Dusina. I can't say which sources I obtained such information from. There are various sources involved. I heard that crimes had been committed, but I really can't confirm that civilians were killed. Similarly, I don't know who these individuals were. And if there were such crimes, if such crimes were committed, I don't know which unit might have been involved in them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's very clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sir, anything that you would have learnt in the Zenica area, in particular, during the period January 1993 and March 1994 would have been what you were told or what you heard; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say, then, that during the period 1993 to 1994, you were not in a position to assist General Hadzihasanovic in any way with respect to the army that he commanded?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
