utterances.text: My position was quite clear. I won't hide the good opinion I have about Mr. Hadzihasanovic. But all I could do was speak to him about the situation, about his position and my position, about the position other people were in, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And subsequently, you would not be in a position to analyse whether or not the situation was a difficult one for the general to handle?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, the situation was difficult, and I thought Mr. Hadzihasanovic's task was an impossible one. I can also provide you some information relayed through the media. There were addresses to the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the commander of the army. I asked him, in the case of people who had come to Zenica without having been invited there, in the case of people who weren't needed by that town and in the case of people who were frightening all the people in Zenica, I asked him to ensure that they left Zenica as soon as possible. And I think I mentioned that Mr. Hadzihasanovic's position was a very difficult one and that if politicians didn't help him and if clear positions weren't defined, I said that the situation would be extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The newspaper articles and reports that you just referred to, that in itself, would you agree with me, is a form of propaganda, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was a matter of propaganda or that propaganda was being spread for the sake of one group of people or one people. I remember a public address, and on that occasion, foreigners probably killed a humanitarian worker and wounded two others. The reaction was very fierce, and the situation in Zenica was such that a request for aid was made. I think that sending one person to Zenica and not offering an overall form of aid couldn't help to resolve the difficulties that we were encountering in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My learned friend showed you a document, DH1423, and it referred to what you described as propaganda. And my question to you is this: How do you assess when something is propaganda and when it's not?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally, if you know what the actual situation is, what efforts are being made, in a town where the conditions weren't good for everyone, well, in such a case, then you may know that propaganda is at stake. If someone says there's 16 people representing a church and this doesn't reflect the actual situation, then this is propaganda. If an order is issued to arrest people who really wanted to live together and help everyone, then it's quite clearly propaganda, or this involves the spreading of false information for the HVO or for the HDZ. As I said, if someone says that 16 people are hanged before a church and this isn't true, this is propaganda. So it might be difficult for people to distinguish between propaganda and the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That's precisely the point. If somebody says that "I was maltreated and ill-treated in the Zenica music school," do you analyse that or assess it as propaganda?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: That depends on the person who provides me with that information. If I was told about this from an HDZ local politician, I would have been suspicious. But if I heard about this from a citizen of Zenica or from one of my employees or a family member, one of my employees or from one of my family members, I would have believed such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Justice Adamovic, of which my colleague referred to, testified before this Court that several reports were made to him with respect to detainees who were mistreated at the Zenica music school. Would you consider that to be propaganda?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: If Judge Adamovic said and had arguments to support it I wouldn't consider that to be propaganda. I don't see why he would spread such propaganda. But I think that Mr. Adamovic was a judge in the military court, and he could process such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Several witnesses came before this Trial Chamber and themselves testified of mistreatment and abuse in the Zenica music school, for example. You were not a member of the military at the time. You were just a director of an ironworks company. But you indicated to this Court that, as far as you're aware, that was far from the truth. On what basis did you make the statement that the testimony that was given is far from the truth? On what basis?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. I don't know who said that there was torture. But the music school doesn't have the capacity for detaining prisoners. One would have heard the sound of torture. The music school is 20 metres from the court, 30 metres from the police station, from the municipal building, and I must say that I have my doubts about such statements. As I said, men who were arrested for stupid reasons, they were taken away, they were interrogated, records of some kind were taken. I felt that people were playing at war, et cetera. But as to what has been stated about the music school, I can't confirm such statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So, in truth and in fact, sir, you cannot really assist us with respect to what happened at the music school. So in fact, you cannot say that it is not true. It's sufficient for you to say you have your doubts, am I correct, but to say that it's not true, you couldn't really tell this Court that, could you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: If I had reliable information, then I would inform the Chamber of the fact. Citizens in Zenica provided me with information. They were involved in providing food, heating, et cetera, and they relied on the company I was in charge of, and I would certainly have heard from them that such things were happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that the HVO commander had written to General Hadzihasanovic complaining about the treatment of the Croats and the Serbs in Zenica? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I'd like to tell you about something I do know about. I know --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Before we go into what you know, can I just finish this part, and then we'll go into what you know, please, so that we don't lose the train of what's happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the Chamber's permission, could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 519, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry to interrupt. I know that the time is ticking on, but before the witness is asked to look at this document, which he in all likelihood would not recognise, because it's not one that involved his activities, as he has described them in 1993, but I did want to object to this document being shown to the witness, because this matter wasn't dealt with at all in the examination-in-chief, by either the counsel for the first defendant or by us. We asked no questions about these matters. And in our submission, there's no basis for asking the witness about these matters. There might be other witnesses who could answer these questions, but certainly not this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A little -- a minor legal issue. The Defence says that in the examination-in-chief, they did not raise the issue that is referred to in this document. Before you're granted leave to put your question to the witness, if leave is granted, what is the purpose of this document? What are you seeking to establish in relation to what the witness has said so far?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned friend raised the issue of the protection of the Croats with the witness in her examination-in-chief. Further, the witness has said, time and time again, that the -- described the situation in Zenica, and he spoke to the fact that he had his doubts as to whether or not certain things transpired in Zenica in January of 1993 and thereafter, until March 1994. And he even went further to say that if Judge Adamovic had received complaints, he wouldn't doubt it, but he hadn't received any. And the purpose here is to highlight to the witness the situation as it was in Zenica, even though he was present and even though he was there, clearly he wasn't aware of what's going on. And perhaps maybe if we were to show him a document by the other side requesting some kind of assistance, maybe it may jog his memory. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have two members of the Defence who are rising to their feet at the same time. This must be very important. You may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is important, because it steps out of all the frameworks of the right to cross-examination and it goes beyond practice hitherto in this Tribunal. The document in no way can refresh the witness's memory with respect to what he was saying, and so I join in the arguments presented previously by our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps the problem is that my learned colleague got the number of the document wrong, because this relates to Visoko and does not refer to the situation in Zenica at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it the right document, then, Prosecutor? Because this document refers to the municipality of Visoko. So have you got the right document or did you wish to make a comparison? But then that complicates matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That is exactly the point, Mr. President. I wanted to be able to read, 1, 2, 3, 4, the fourth paragraph, the two lines there, and compare it with the document that was used by my learned friend for the witness to give us his interpretation of what transpired then, or rather, what he knows transpired.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I never showed the witness any similar document, anything along these lines, so I don't know how my learned colleague is referring to what I asked the witness and basing her question on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, madam Benjamin. The Defence never showed a document of this type. But since we have the difficulty, perhaps you could ask a question first and then link it up with what you've been saying hitherto.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Firstly, Mr. President, we wish to apologise. The document was dated as 519, P519 in our documents. But I'm told by the case manager that this is 591 and not 519. My apologies. That's the first thing. We have a written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we've lost almost ten minutes over that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: We won't allow you to lose any more minutes. We're almost to the end. So I would withdraw the document from the witness. And I will just -- I would just ask the witness to conclude for me if, in his position as commander, as director of the ironworks, if he thinks that he's in a position to explain to this Court fully what transpired in Zenica in 1993 and March 1994.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to say that the question asked me a moment ago is going to help me to answer the question and explain the situation. Let me say that I understood the situation in Zenica very well. My grandfather was born there, my father was born there, I lived there, and I have two children who are going to stay on and live there. So I have lived together with the town. And I'd like to say that probably Madam Prosecutor does not know the situation in town, what it was like; whereas I do and I felt it on my own skin. I could breathe it and feel it. Up until March 1993, that's my second point, when the conflict between the BH army and the HVO broke out, the position of the Croats in Zenica was incomparably better than was the position of the Bosniaks. The position taken by Mr. Hadzihasanovic was very difficult. He was being accused, both by the Croatian side and the Bosniak side, and I know that he was directly accused and blamed for the fact that the HVO had taken over the towns of Zepce, Busovaca, and others, where the percentage or the population ratio was roughly 50/50. And they considered that his efforts to solve the situation peacefully led to the fact that all the inhabitants of those towns who were not Croats were expelled, and that in the space of just a few days, they all poured into Zenica. Let me try and explain what my position was in Zenica until March 1993, briefly. I am certain that I helped people in Zenica. I helped the Croats, perhaps even more than any political party was able to do, or any military formation, for that matter, which I think had different intentions vis-a-vis the Croats in Zenica. The Zenica ironworks was a company which had money on its accounts outside the country, and it took upon itself to supply the town with food, to a certain extent. From 1992 until 1994, the company money was used to buy and bring in to Zenica about 50.000 tonnes of food. That's one point. Let me explain. Let me explain the difficulties we had in importing this food, which was used for the entire Zenica population.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sir, without being rude in any way and without interrupting you, time is against us, and as much as I think we would all like to hear the history, my question was really, really specific. I just wanted to know, not being a member of the military, if you felt that you were confident enough to give an account or an analysis of what took place in Zenica during the conflict in 1993 to 1994. Very specific and very short, to the point. And if you could just answer that, then that will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: Not about events on the battlefield, but as to events in town, the situation in town and the relationships there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But not events in the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this ends the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, additional questions, Your Honour. There was just mistake which I think was put right. A document on page 76, line 24, was denoted as P685, whereas -- or rather, it was 685 and not 655, which is what it said in the transcript. But I didn't want to interrupt my learned colleague to give that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions from me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I see that there is one -- document 1423. Would you like that tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I address myself to the Prosecution. The Defence is asking for the admission of document 1243 -- 1423, which is a propaganda document. It is number 4, and it is an HVO document. 1423 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has objections to DH1423, for the obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what are the obvious reasons? Because it might not be that evident to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document is -- this witness is not the author of this document, in the first instance. The witness was only able to give an assessment of what he read on the document as what it is. And it is my opinion, or the opinion of the Prosecution, that the proper foundation was not laid by the Defence in order to have the document tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the Judges will give the matter their thought later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd just like to repeat: The witness was in Zenica. He knew about the situation. He quoted instances of propaganda that was used as a system. So all the grounds upon which this Trial Chamber adopted documents previously are met with this particular document, so I think it can be admitted into evidence. And I'm surprised that my learned colleague raised the question in the first place, because I'm sure there have been at least 900 documents that have been tendered into evidence without a witness, and I think this is very clear grounds for having the document accepted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to deliberate, and we'll be giving a ruling in due course. Witness, you have understood that there are no further questions for you. Your testimony has come to an end. You will be able to go home quickly. I thank you for having come to the Tribunal and given us valuable information on the situation that existed at that time. I would also like to thank you for having answered the questions asked you, and I wish you bon voyage back home, and of course best wishes for you at the head of the company which you manage. Thank you. I'm going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for next week, let's hear from the Defence first.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on Monday, according to our schedule -- may we go into private session, please, because we're going to mention witness names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you wish to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could very briefly, Mr. President. You alluded to this earlier this morning, and unfortunately, although she is not here today or at this moment, the Prosecution would certainly like to put on the record the fact that we certainly found working with Ms. Godart to be a very good experience in terms of her professionalism and the hard work and dedication that she brought, I think, to both parties in terms of assisting us with this trial and the Prosecution thought on her last day it was simply appropriate to point out for the record that certainly the Prosecution, and I'm sure our colleagues from the Defence, would agree that she will be sorrily missed in this trial and we all wish her the best of luck and I would respectfully ask that that be passed on to her in the event that she is not listening and following at this point in time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should fully like to support what my learned colleague has just said. We endorse it. We value highly the good relationship and assistance we have always received from her during the trial, Ms. Godart, and we wish her all the best in her new work in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall convey your best wishes to Ms. Godart in the next few minutes, and I'm sure she will appreciate it highly. I apologise to the interpreters and technicians for keeping them late today, but we could not act otherwise. We resume on Monday at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
